 Taiwan shuts US$5 trillion stock market as Typhoon Champi nears

 | 11:15 AM MYT

 Taiwan Stock Exchange displays its new logo in a ceiling vault of its building in Taipei, Taiwan July 11, 2023 Joe Wang/TWSE/Handout via REUTERS/File Photo 
 Taiwan shut its $5 trillion stock market, schools and offices on Friday as Typhoon Champi barreled toward the island, bringing heavy rain and damaging winds that disrupted flights.
 Champi was packing top sustained winds of 155 kilometers (96 miles) an hour, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane, according to the island’s weather agency, after weakening over the past 24 hours from super typhoon strength. The storm was around 340 kilometers southeast of Taipei’s Taoyuan International Airport as of 10:15 a.m. Friday local time, the bureau added.
 Most of Taiwan’s cities and counties shut offices and schools for safety on Friday, while the storm had already killed one person and injured 94, according to government statements. More than 900 international and domestic flights were canceled on Friday, along with some train services.
 Taiwan’s stock exchange, the fifth-largest globally, will also be closed Monday for a holiday, giving the island an additional trading gap compared with other markets in the region. The tech-heavy exchange, along with those in South Korea and Japan, has sold off recently as investors track earnings from global tech giants.
 Cooler ocean waters and increasing wind shear will steadily shave some intensity from Champi, but it remains a very large cyclone with an expansive wind field, according to the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center. The storm is forecast to pass just east of Taipei early Saturday before curving northeast along mainland China’s east coast on its way toward Japan’s Kyushu.
 "The risks that matter now are rain and the size of the wind field,” said James Caron, director of meteorological operations for North America and Asia at Atmospheric G2. "The 185-miles-per-hour peak is behind us.”
 Champi achieved super typhoon strength earlier in the week, making it the 10th to reach that level in the northwest Pacific Ocean this season. That’s double the long-term average and just shy of a record 13 during 2015’s El Niño, according to the Hong Kong Observatory. Storms tend to form farther east during the climate phenomenon, giving them more time to accumulate energy over warm, open waters as they churn toward land. - Bloomberg
